candidates.speaker: James White
candidates.proposition: Christ's substitutionary atonement preserves divine justice while making genuine mercy and grace available to sinners.
candidates.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted opening presentation and moderator-established speaking order identify James White as the speaker.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This directly states the Christian account's central claimed advantage: forgiveness is achieved without separating God's mercy from his law and justice.
candidates.contextSummary: After describing humanity as enslaved to sin, White explains why strict justice alone offers no rescue and presents substitution as the means by which justice and mercy coincide.

candidates.speaker: James White
candidates.proposition: Titus presents Jesus as divine Savior whose voluntary, sufficient self-giving redeems sinners, grants righteousness, and produces purified people zealous for good deeds.
candidates.attributionBasis: The sustained opening presentation, first-person references, and moderator-established order consistently identify James White.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The passage supplies the principal New Testament foundation for the pro account of Christ's identity, atoning work, sufficiency, imputed righteousness, and resulting moral transformation.
candidates.contextSummary: White closely develops a passage from Titus, connecting Christ's divine identity and voluntary incarnation to complete redemption, righteous standing, purification, and good works motivated by love rather than merit.

candidates.speaker: James White
candidates.proposition: Direct forgiveness without atonement appears to leave God's violated law unanswered and offers fallen people no secure basis for peace with a holy God.
candidates.attributionBasis: The material remains within James White's uninterrupted opening statement immediately before the moderator announces rebuttals.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This frames the debate's decisive comparative challenge by arguing that the direct-forgiveness model cannot jointly account for divine law, human fallenness, and assurance of reconciliation.
candidates.contextSummary: Near the end of his opening, White contrasts the two systems by questioning unatoned forgiveness, human ability to satisfy divine standards, and the foundation for peace with God.

candidates.speaker: Shabir Ally
candidates.proposition: God may forgive repentant sinners without compromising holiness or justice, because equitable mercy and the release of debt are legitimate divine prerogatives.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly introduces Shabir Ally's rebuttal, and the passage begins with his direct response to James White.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is the con side's central answer to the demand for atonement, defending direct forgiveness through divine prerogative, evenhanded mercy, and biblical commands and prayers concerning forgiveness.
candidates.contextSummary: Ally answers White's example of a forgiven murderer, uses a Gospel parable to defend divine generosity, and argues from biblical interpersonal forgiveness and debt remission that forgiveness need not entail punishment.

candidates.speaker: Shabir Ally
candidates.proposition: Human beings need not be morally perfect to be judged righteous, since good can outweigh wrongdoing and biblical figures are called righteous despite ordinary shortcomings.
candidates.attributionBasis: This passage continues Shabir Ally's uninterrupted rebuttal under the clearly announced rebuttal speaking order.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move attacks the anthropology that makes substitution indispensable, replacing total moral inability with accountable moral agency and qualified righteousness recognized by God.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: White's earlier opening argument that pervasive depravity makes human deeds unacceptable before God's holiness.

candidates.contextSummary: Ally rejects an absolute account of depravity, invokes the Qur'anic weighting of good and bad deeds, and cites biblical persons described as righteous without claiming that they were faultless.

candidates.speaker: Shabir Ally
candidates.proposition: Substitutionary justification is especially Pauline and gains support in later Gospels, whose post-Pauline dating permits influence from Paul's already established theology.
candidates.attributionBasis: The argument is delivered continuously by Shabir Ally during his moderator-announced rebuttal period.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This challenges the scriptural grounding and historical priority of the pro account by treating its Gospel support as a later development influenced by Pauline teaching.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: White's reliance on Paul and later Gospel material as a unified biblical basis for substitutionary salvation.

candidates.contextSummary: Ally argues that White's Pauline and Johannine citations fit a developmental thesis, then defends dates placing Mark after Paul by appealing to scholars identified as conservative Christians.

candidates.speaker: Shabir Ally
candidates.proposition: Divine enablement does not eliminate the believer's obligation to work out salvation, so salvation cannot be treated as already guaranteed solely by Jesus's substitutionary death.
candidates.attributionBasis: The passage is the closing portion of Shabir Ally's uninterrupted rebuttal and ends immediately before the next speaker begins.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move directly contests the sufficiency and guarantee claimed for atonement by maintaining that scripturally required human action remains necessary to salvation.
candidates.contextSummary: Ally accepts that God may enable good action but argues that the command to work out salvation still assigns an indispensable role to human conduct inconsistent with an already guaranteed result.

candidates.speaker: James White
candidates.proposition: Working out salvation means expressing a salvation already possessed through God's transforming activity, not earning it or supplementing Christ's completed work.
candidates.attributionBasis: A clear speaker transition follows Ally's thanks, and the announced rebuttal order identifies the new speaker as James White.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This preserves the pro model's coherence between grace and moral effort by construing good works as divinely produced consequences rather than conditions that complete salvation.
candidates.contextSummary: White distinguishes working out from working for salvation, links the command to sanctification and good deeds, and rejects the claim that Paul contradicts himself within a consistent biblical theology.

candidates.speaker: James White
candidates.proposition: Commands that sinners forgive one another do not show that God may forgive without atonement, because forgiven human debtors and the holy lawgiver occupy fundamentally different positions.
candidates.attributionBasis: The passage continues James White's uninterrupted rebuttal following the clearly marked transition from Shabir Ally.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This directly blocks the principal biblical analogy offered for unatoned forgiveness by distinguishing interpersonal mercy among sinners from God's response to violations of his own law.
candidates.contextSummary: White argues that humans must forgive because they themselves require and receive forgiveness, whereas God is the sinless creator and lawgiver against whom the offense has been committed.

candidates.speaker: James White
candidates.proposition: A discretionary or curve-based model of forgiveness makes salvation arbitrary and disconnects God's standards from his nature, whereas Christ's perfect righteousness satisfies those standards securely.
candidates.attributionBasis: This is a continuous portion of James White's rebuttal, with explicit references back to Shabir Ally's preceding examples.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move sharpens the comparative coherence test by contrasting uncertain discretionary mercy with an atonement claimed to fulfill a law inseparable from God's own nature.
candidates.contextSummary: White interprets Ally's professor analogy as grading on a curve, questions the resulting uncertainty and arbitrariness, and contrasts it with believers standing through Christ's perfect righteousness.
